Article Title: Why personal-guarantor recoveries are so tiny — and why Chandra’s was tinier still
Article Text:
AI illustration

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Get the full story

Does it work? A personal guarantor was once facing claims of over Rs 330 crore. She offered … Rs 1 lakh

How much can a personal guarantee really expose you to? In law, potentially the whole unpaid debt

Subhash Chandra’s proposed repayment of a little over Rs 6 crore against more than Rs 22,000 crore of admitted claims worked out to less than 0.03%.That looks exceptionally small. And it was. But personal-guarantor insolvency cases have produced very low recoveries more generally.Data from the insolvency regulator shows that nearly 5,200 applications have been filed against personal guarantors since the process came into force in 2019-20. Only around 64 have so far ended in repayment plans approved by creditors and the tribunal. Across those cases, lenders recovered a little under Rs 235 crore — roughly 1% of their admitted claims.So the larger problem is not specific to Chandra — on September 1, a specially constituted five-member bench of the NCLT stayed the order approving it anyway — but that the amount a person guarantees can be very different from what is actually available by the time lenders try to collect.A personal guarantee creates a liability. It does not, by itself, preserve the wealth behind that liability.When lenders take a guarantee, they can look at the guarantor’s assets, liabilities, credit history and other guarantees already given. But unless specific property is separately pledged or mortgaged, those assets are not locked away for the lender.But years can pass between a loan being made and a guarantee being invoked.In the meantime, assets can fall in value, be sold, be pledged elsewhere or be used to meet other liabilities.Chandra’s case shows how large that gap can become. Net-worth certificates submitted to banks in 2017 and 2018 put his worth at more than Rs 40,000 crore. During the insolvency proceedings, he said his assets were worth a little under Rs 32 crore, most of them already mortgaged, leaving around Rs 6.5 crore.(Chandra has disputed the earlier figure, saying it did not represent what he personally owned.)If the problem is that the wealth behind the guarantee can disappear or become unavailable, one way to make guarantees more useful is to make sure some of that wealth remains in place.Lenders can, for instance, require a guarantor to maintain a minimum net worth or a minimum amount of liquid assets while the loan is outstanding. Such covenants are used elsewhere. One US guarantee filed with the securities regulator required the guarantors to maintain at least $90 million in net worth and $8 million in liquid assets, and restricted transfers that would take them below those levels.Another option is to back the guarantee with a specific asset. A house, for instance, can be mortgaged against the guarantee. India already allows this, and such arrangements give lenders something more concrete than a general promise backed by whatever assets happen to remain later.There is also the question of finding those assets once insolvency begins. Rules introduced in 2026 widened the disclosures that can be sought from personal guarantors to include assets held through nominees, trusts and companies, as well as assets they control or benefit from without formally owning them. Another rule allows certain undervalued transactions intended to put assets beyond creditors’ reach to be reversed.None of these measures can ensure full recovery. A guarantor can still genuinely lose wealth.But they can narrow the gap between what a guarantee appears to be worth when a loan is made and what lenders find when they finally try to enforce it.Why did the government drag personal guarantors into insolvency at all? Not just to recover more — but to make corporate borrowing harder to shrug off
Article Summary: Nearly 5,200 applications have been filed against personal guarantors since the process came into force in 2019-20. Only around 64 have so far ended in repayment plans approved by creditors and the tribunal. Across those cases, lenders recovered a little under Rs 235 crore — roughly 1% of their admitted claims.

NEW DELHI: India and Belgium on Thursday signed a series of MoUs and agreements aimed at expanding bilateral cooperation across renewable energy, defence, trade, investment, maritime affairs, critical minerals, semiconductors and research, as Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever held talks in New Delhi.The agreements were exchanged in the presence of PM Modi and De Wever at Hyderabad House, with the two sides seeking to turn the longstanding India-Belgium relationship into a broader strategic and economic partnership.PM Modi said the two countries had agreed to strengthen cooperation in several emerging areas, including startups, maritime capacity building, universities and research, while also working towards a Migration and Mobility Partnership Agreement to facilitate the movement of talent."Today, we agreed to strengthen connections between our startups and enhance capacity building in the maritime sector. We will also reinforce cooperation in the university and research sectors, and we will soon sign a Migration and Mobility Partnership Agreement to facilitate the movement of talent. Today we also held detailed discussions on regional and global developments. Both India and Belgium believe in the rule of law, dialogue, and diplomacy..."The Prime Minister also highlighted the renewable energy MoU signed during the visit, saying it would provide fresh momentum to bilateral cooperation on sustainability. The two countries have additionally decided to enhance cooperation in the processing and recycling of critical minerals."Defence and security cooperation is a key pillar of our relationship. Today, we have agreed to enhance military exchanges and training cooperation between the two countries. Agreements reached between our governments and defence industries will open up new opportunities for defence co-development and co-production. We will also further strengthen intelligence sharing and cooperation against crime between our respective agencies. A clean energy future and reliable supply chains are our shared priorities. The MoU on renewable energy signed today will give new momentum to our cooperation on sustainability. We have decided to enhance cooperation in the processing and recycling of critical minerals. Belgium's expertise in semiconductors and India's scale complement each other; in this regard, we will work together to integrate Belgium's IMEC Institute with India's semiconductor ecosystem. People-to-people ties are the greatest strength of our relationship."The two sides also discussed ways to strengthen economic ties following the conclusion of the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement earlier this year. PM Modi said India and Belgium had taken several steps to translate the opportunities created by the agreement into concrete economic outcomes."Earlier this year, we concluded a historic Free Trade Agreement between India and the European Union. This unprecedented cooperation between two of the world's largest democratic powers will further strengthen global stability, growth, and shared prosperity. India's sustained economic progress and this agreement have opened up new possibilities for our economic ties. Today, we have taken several significant steps to translate these possibilities into concrete results. We have established an 'Investment Fast-Track Mechanism' in India for Belgian companies. We have decided to make the India-Belgium Business Forum a regular mechanism. We will enhance synergy between the financial, fintech, and regulatory institutions of both nations, and through these measures, we will realize the goal of doubling bilateral trade over the next five years"Defence cooperation emerged as another key component of the agreements and discussions. PM Modi said India and Belgium had agreed to increase military exchanges and training, while government and defence industry agreements would create opportunities for co-development and co-production of defence equipment.He also said the two countries would strengthen intelligence sharing and cooperation between their agencies to combat crime.PM Modi said India and Belgium were also working together on modern defence equipment and cited the Zorawar tank as an example of the expanding partnership."I had the opportunity to visit Belgium ten years ago, and I am delighted to see the remarkable progress our partnership has made over the past decade. Today, the scope of our cooperation has expanded beyond traditional sectors to encompass strategic areas such as defense and clean energy. We are collaborating on modern defence equipment, such as the Zorawar tank. We are also developing one of the world's largest green ammonia projects in Kakinada, Andhra Pradesh. "On clean energy and technology, PM Modi said the renewable energy agreement would strengthen cooperation on sustainability, while the proposed integration of Belgium's IMEC Institute with India's semiconductor ecosystem would combine Belgian expertise with India's scale.The two countries also discussed critical minerals, particularly their processing and recycling, as both sides look to build more reliable supply chains.PM Modi said the latest agreements marked an expansion of ties beyond traditional areas such as diamonds and trade."Last month, Belgium and the Netherlands jointly hosted the Hockey World Cup. I extend my heartiest congratulations to you for the magnificent organization of this World Cup. I also commend our players for their hard work and performance. Diamonds have long linked India and Belgium. Today, we are transforming this historic bond into a comprehensive partnership. I am confident that our discussions today mark the beginning of a new chapter in our bilateral relations. .."The Prime Minister also placed the bilateral engagement in the context of ongoing global conflicts and geopolitical uncertainty, saying India and Belgium supported efforts towards peace while sharing a commitment to combating terrorism."... Whether it is Ukraine or West Asia, we support all efforts towards an early end to conflict and the establishment of peace; furthermore, eradicating terrorism in all its forms is our shared commitment. Last month, Belgium and the Netherlands jointly hosted the Hockey World Cup. I extend my heartiest congratulations to you for the magnificent organization of this World Cup. I also commend our players for their hard work and performance. Diamonds have long linked India and Belgium. Today, we are transforming this historic bond into a comprehensive partnership. I am confident that our discussions today mark the beginning of a new chapter in our bilateral relations..."PM Modi said the broader global environment remained challenging, with conflicts affecting food and fuel security as well as supply chains. He said India's economy had continued to maintain its momentum despite the uncertainty."The world is currently going through a period of great upheaval. Conflict situations persist in various parts of the globe, and uncertainty is impacting sectors ranging from food and fuel to supply chains. Even amidst this challenging environment, the Indian economy has maintained its momentum; we recorded a growth rate of 7.8% in the last quarter. Today, India's growth story is becoming a source of confidence and new opportunities for the world. "The agreements and discussions came during De Wever's first visit to India as Belgian Prime Minister. He is in the country from September 2 to 4 at the invitation of PM Modi. His visit is also the first by a Belgian Prime Minister to India in two decades.De Wever, who took office in February 2025, is accompanied by Belgium's Minister of Defence and Foreign Trade, Theo Francken, along with a high-level delegation of officials and business leaders, including representatives from the Belgian defence industry.Earlier on Thursday, Francken held the India-Belgium Defence Ministers' Meeting with Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, where both sides discussed expanding defence cooperation and greater engagement between their defence industries."The world is witnessing a time of great geopolitical and economic turmoil. Most of it is not our doing, but we have to handle the challenges. In such situations, meeting a friend and partner like you provides a useful opportunity to exchange views and perspectives," Singh said.Singh said the recently held India-Belgium Strategic Dialogue had provided a framework for taking the bilateral partnership forward, particularly in defence and security."We welcome greater cooperation with Belgian and Indian defence companies," he said.Francken, meanwhile, called for deeper cooperation with India, highlighting the country's technological capabilities and saying Belgium needed partners such as India for future projects."We can learn so much from you. You are a high-technology country. You are one of the most densely populated countries, and we really need to work together because Belgium is an old Western European country with a lot of technology, but we need countries like India. We need to collaborate on future projects, and for Belgium, this is the way forward"Francken also referred to Belgium's economic mission to India led by Princess Astrid in March 2025, describing it as a first step towards a renewed relationship between the two countries.He said the mission had helped generate momentum in bilateral ties, with contracts being signed on collaboration projects within 18 months."That is amazing. This means that we worked hard, that our people worked hard, and that we can go further in this pathway."The Belgian minister also said De Wever's visit had a packed agenda focused on expanding bilateral cooperation."I'm very happy to be here with our Prime Minister. For first time in more than 20 years a Belgian Prime Minister is visiting your beautiful country. We have a busy, busy schedule with lot of signing ceremonies, a lot of good talks with the Prime Minister…"Francken said Belgium and India could address the geopolitical challenges facing the world through greater friendship and partnership."I think it's totally right when you talk about geopolitical challenges that we have to meet. We didn't organise them, we didn't always want them, but we need to be realistic, and we need to go further. And we can do this in friendship and partnership between Belgium and India."The latest agreements build on growing economic engagement between the two countries. A Belgian Economic Mission led by Princess Astrid in March 2025 brought together 338 participants from companies, chambers of commerce, academia and public institutions and resulted in 38 MoUs.De Wever also paid tributes to Mahatma Gandhi at Rajghat on Thursday, where he laid a wreath and offered flowers before signing the visitor's book.The Belgian Prime Minister's visit is aimed at further strengthening bilateral ties and expanding cooperation across trade, investment, defence, technology and connectivity, while also giving fresh momentum to India's engagement with the European Union and Europe.

The two sides sought to turn the longstanding India-Belgium relationship into a broader strategic and economic partnership. Article Title: More teachers, better access, fewer pupils: India’s government school paradox
Article Text:
Gujarat Government school

From buffaloes and buckets to what the national numbers say

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe that the government should prioritize improving infrastructure in government schools over expanding private school options? Yes, infrastructure should be prioritized No, private school options are more important 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Nearly 1 lakh fewer govt schools, but access improves on paper

Nearly 1 lakh less government school in 10 years

Govt schools are losing pupils even as the system improves

The changing mix

More teachers nationally, TOI finds the gaps locally

Single teacher school decreasing

More children stay on, but Class X remains a fault line

Drop-outs decreasing

Digital access surges, but TOI finds a different classroom reality

Toilets on paper, TOI finds the functionality gap on the ground

The basic-access gap remains

Basic access gap remains

Schools are back in focus. In larger policy discussions and political debates. The Opposition, emboldened by its NEET protest victory, is looking to up the ante by exposing ramshackle school infrastructure in different states, starting with Rajasthan. TOI ground reports, too, have found gross inadequacies in government schools across different parts of the state. Particularly jarring is the fact that in Kota , widely called the coaching capital of India, many government schools are in a dilapidated state. wider ground report by TOI reporters across the country found that Rajasthan was hardly an outlier. In Bihar, nearly 200 children from four classes were sharing a single room at one school while cattle occupied two others. In Uttarakhand, leaking roofs meant buckets and umbrellas had become classroom fixtures. In Madhya Pradesh, TOI found schools struggling with teacher shortages and unsafe buildings. Keralam was a prominent exception to this broader picture.However, the fact remains that in a country of 1.4 billion people, structural gaps are perhaps expected, if certainly not desired. A good metric of how much the school system has improved over the years is to look at the data furnished by the central government and its allied agencies.The pan-India numbers make for interesting reading. Rajasthan had 7,200 single-teacher schools in 2025-26, while only 36.4% of schools reported ramps with handrails and 26.3% had toilets tailored for Children with Special Needs (CwSN).The country has nearly a lakh fewer government schools than it did a decade ago, and those schools are losing pupils. It also has more teachers, far fewer children in single-teacher schools, more teenagers reaching higher secondary and internet access in about two-thirds of schools. Fewer than half of schools, however, report a toilet designed for children with special needs. Yet despite improvements in many metrics, government-school enrolment is falling.Most of what is known about India's schools comes from UDISE+, the Unified District Information System for Education Plus. It is an annual, census-like administrative database covering schools across management types. Schools report on their pupils, teachers and infrastructure, from enrolment and staffing to toilets, electricity, ramps, computers and internet access, and they are incorporated into the Union education ministry's national school statistics.The system grew out of UDISE, created in 2012-13 by merging separate elementary and secondary databases. UDISE+ became its online successor from 2018-19. The government uses it to locate infrastructure gaps, and states draw on it when seeking support for classrooms, toilets, drinking water, electricity, libraries and digital facilities under schemes such as Samagra Shiksha.A school can figure in the database as open and equipped with a particular facility, but reality can be very different. TOI's visits across states repeatedly brought out that distinction.India had 11,04,796 government schools in 2015-16. Ten years later, UDISE+ records 10,05,245, a difference of 99,551 schools or 9%. The rider is that a school leaving the UDISE count can reflect closure, merger, rationalisation, reclassification or other administrative change.The decline is stark in some states. Madhya Pradesh had 1,21,976 government schools in 2015-16; by 2025-26 the count was 91,199, a reduction of 30,777. Uttar Pradesh fell from 1,62,645 to 1,37,103, a reduction of 25,542. Together, the two states account for about 56.6% of the national net decline over the decade.There have also been changes in school mapping and verification, with UDISE+ replacing the older UDISE system from 2018-19. Questioned in Parliament, the Centre has said that decisions on opening, closing and rationalising schools lie largely with states and Union territories, while the Right to Education framework requires elementary schools to remain accessible within prescribed neighbourhood limits.Between 2018-19 and 2024-25, the Gross Access Ratio rose from 88.24% to 95.35% at the secondary level and from 65.05% to 94.97% at higher secondary. GAR measures the proportion of habitations or villages with a school available within the prescribed distance; it is not an enrolment ratio. So although there are fewer schools, the measured access ratio has improved. This is also part of the government's defence.Government-school enrolment fell from 12.75 crore in 2023-24 to 11.89 crore in 2025-26, nearly 85.9 lakh fewer pupils in just two years, a decline of 6.7%. Over the same period, enrolment in private unaided schools rose from 9.00 crore to 9.89 crore, an increase of about 88.3 lakh, or 9.8%. The thinning out is also visible over a decade with average enrolment per government school falling from about 132 pupils in 2014-15 to 120 in 2024-25, a decline of roughly 9%; the latest UDISE+ figures put it at about 118 in 2025-26.One figure from the government's own parliamentary reply captures the scale of it. In 2024-25, government institutions accounted for 68.9% of all schools in India but 49.2% of all enrolment.A movement this large might be expected to have triggered a substantial investigation. On July 29, 2026, the government was asked why government-school enrolment had fallen from about 12.8 crore to 11.9 crore while private enrolment rose from around 9 crore to 9.9 crore.The ministry confirmed the numbers but did not cite or summarise such an assessment in its reply. Instead, it listed the interventions being made to strengthen government education.NITI Aayog's 2026 UDISE+-based review says the broader decline in enrolment through 2024-25 is partly attributable to demographic shifts, particularly falling fertility and a smaller school-age population, alongside school consolidation and challenges in retaining pupils at higher levels.Ranabir Bhattacharyya, teacher-in-charge of the English-medium primary section of Chetla Boys' High School in Kolkata, points to some of the practical issues with UDISE+ and also offers context for the dwindling numbers. He says the data had many issues at one point, but the pipeline has increasingly been made more robust as the government seeks to bring all students onto the platform to roll out various developmental schemes aimed at schoolchildren.He alleges that there was earlier an incentive in certain quarters to inflate pupil numbers, but says tighter vigilance has reduced that tendency and the numbers now being reflected are closer to reality. Ranabir, however, flags other problems like the website can be difficult to use and often suffers technical glitches, while the absence of additional staff increases the workload of those responsible for keeping the data updated. As a result, underreporting can happen too, according to him.India had 96.96 lakh teachers in 2020-21 and 102.73 lakh in 2025-26, nearly 5.77 lakh additional teachers in five years. Single-teacher schools fell from 1,10,971 in 2023-24 to 1,00,843 in 2025-26, and the number of children enrolled in them dropped more steeply still, from 39.94 lakh to 29.12 lakh. Nearly 11 lakh fewer children are now in such schools.But the national improvement hides striking state differences. Andhra Pradesh alone has 16,357 single-teacher schools; Jharkhand has 9,827, Maharashtra 9,269, Karnataka 8,042 and Uttar Pradesh 7,874. Those five states together account for just over half of India's 1,00,843 single-teacher schools.And this is one area where the statistical picture intersects sharply with what TOI reporters saw. In Madhya Pradesh, TOI found 70 children and one teacher operating from a single dilapidated room at a school in Bhopal's Kolar, while students in Classes XI and XII at a PM SHRI school in Mandla had gone without teachers for newly introduced streams for a year.Uttarakhand has 2,655 single-teacher schools, about 11.8% of its entire school network, alongside its unusually high proportion of very small schools. The Centre acknowledges the problem. It has told Parliament that recruitment and postings are primarily state responsibilities; and that it repeatedly presses states on faster recruitment and redeployment while supporting them under Samagra Shiksha.Ranabir highlights another issue involving children of migrant labourers. He says that when a student shifts from one school to another, the subsequent UDISE+ entry does not always move smoothly as it requires manual intervention. West Bengal School Education Minister Dipak Barman, speaking to TOI, says many private schools in the state have not uploaded their student lists. Barman says the state is working to get the figures updated. It is hard to know whether similar anomalies exist elsewhere, but if they do, they could significantly undermine the purpose of what the central government is trying to achieve with the UDISE+ platform.The encouraging part is that reported dropout rates are falling. In many states, girl students are incentivised to continue school education. At the same time, higher-secondary Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) rose from 56.2% in 2023-24 to 61.7% in 2025-26, and the secondary dropout rate fell from 14.1% to 9.5% over the same period. Here too, the national number hides enormous variation. Keralam, for instance, reported secondary retention of 99.1% in 2025-26.For many from financially weaker sections, there is a significant opportunity cost to staying in school after Class X. The government has therefore deployed a range of measures to keep more students in the system. Parliamentary replies point to PM POSHAN, residential schools and hostels, KGBVs, transport assistance, free textbooks and uniforms, enrolment campaigns and vocational education, and more recently to Vidya Samiksha Kendras and APAAR IDs as tools for tracking students who drop out or move between schools.In step with the government's Digital India push, digital infrastructure has expanded rapidly. In 2020-21, 24.5% of schools reported internet access; by 2025-26, 67.4% did. Computer availability rose from 41.3% to 69.9%. The approved budget for ICT labs, smart classrooms and other digital initiatives rose from ₹381.1 crore in 2018-19 to ₹3,221.1 crore in 2025-26.NITI Aayog's 2026 UDISE+-based analysis of functional smart classrooms shows coverage rising from 14.9% of schools in 2021-22 to 30.6% in 2024-25. In other words, even after rapid expansion, nearly seven in ten schools still lacked one.The interstate divide is striking. Punjab reported functional smart classrooms in 80.1% of schools and Delhi in 75.7%; the corresponding figures were only 4.3% in Meghalaya, 5.7% in West Bengal, 14.9% in Bihar and 19.8% in Uttar Pradesh. Tamil Nadu offers the opposite story: its reported coverage went from virtually zero in 2021-22 to 60.8% in 2024-25.TOI's ground visits underline why infrastructure numbers need context. In Uttar Pradesh, schools visited by reporters had toilets and drinking water, but digital resources were missing; in Himachal Pradesh, strong coverage of basic facilities coexisted with substantially weaker smart-classroom and disability-access indicators.Regarding West Bengal's poor showing, Barman says many of the state's UDISE+ figures have not been properly updated and that the government is working to correct them, and is looking to start 2000 smart classrooms in the next one year. He says Bengal expects to be among the top 10 when the next calculation is made.India is now close to universal provision of toilet facilities in schools, at least on paper. UDISE+ reports girls'-toilet availability in 98.5% of girls' and co-educational schools in 2025-26. But availability and functionality are not the same.TOI's ground reporting provides a simple illustration of that distinction. Schools visited in Uttar Pradesh had separate toilets for boys and girls, but reporters found many of them unclean, with teachers blaming the absence of sanitation workers. This issue of not having adequate sanitation staff is something Ranabir also flagged repeatedly.The same NITI Aayog analysis, using 2024-25 data, puts national functional girls'-toilet coverage at 94%, up from 85.17% a decade earlier. Yet the state map remains uneven.In 2024-25, Bihar and Odisha were both at 98.1% functional girls'-toilet coverage and West Bengal at 99.6%, while Rajasthan stood at 87.3%. Meghalaya was at 68.7%, Arunachal Pradesh 73.7% and Manipur 74.5%.In 2020-21, 24.5% of schools reported internet access and 41.3% computers. About 48.3% reported ramps with handrails and 25.3% toilets for children with special needs. By 2025-26, internet availability had reached 67.4% and computers 69.9%. Ramps with handrails were at 58.2%, while CwSN-friendly toilets stood at only 40.1%.The state contrasts are revealing. Himachal Pradesh reports functional electricity in 99.1% of schools and computers in 87.2%, but internet reaches only 66.2% and CwSN-friendly toilets 34%. At the same time, 18.3% of its schools are single-teacher schools and almost half have 30 pupils or fewer.Keralam, the prominent exception in TOI's ground reporting, also stands apart on several UDISE measures. Computer availability is 99.5%, internet access 92.6%, and only 67 schools, about 0.4% of its network, are single-teacher schools. Secondary retention is 99.1%. The state is not without gaps, only around 51.7% of schools report CwSN-friendly toilets but the overall contrast with many other states is striking.The Accessibility Code was notified in 2024, and Samagra Shiksha and PM SHRI provide funds for facility upliftment. Ranabir says funds often come in a trickle or are regularly delayed. As a result, he says, many of these metrics do not improve as smoothly as desired. He also highlights that many rural schools have irregular electricity supply, and hence while internet and other digital facilities are present on paper, reality can be different.Taken together, most of these service and outcome indicators have moved positively. Yet government-school enrolment is falling. That may partly reflect an aspirational society where some parents are looking to private schools for stronger English-language exposure, soft skills, peer networks and perceived advantages in college and beyond. Anecdotally, one can also see the mushrooming of English-medium schools in suburbs and mofussils.But the national data do not by themselves establish why families make these choices. Some of the decline may also reflect cleaner data and ironically even lack of proper uploading of data as pointed out by the Bengal education minister.There is no one-size-fits-all solution for such a large country. The data show substantial progress on several fronts, yet the lived reality may be different in some places. For now, the government will need to tick the boxes on what should be absolutely non-negotiable in terms of core deliverables, including the lacunae exposed in those reports. Winning the larger battle for aspiration may be a challenge for another day, or another decade.
Article Summary: India has nearly a lakh fewer government schools than it did a decade ago, and those schools are losing pupils. The Opposition is looking to up the ante by exposing ramshackle school infrastructure in different states. In Bihar, nearly 200 children from four classes were sharing a single room at one school. In Uttarakhand, leaking roofs meant buckets and umbrellas had become classroom fixtures.

Article Title: Silver prices crash over 40% from Rs 4 lakh/kg high to Rs 2.35 lakh, but buyers are still staying away; bigger problem yet to arrive as 2,000 tonnes ordered by Indian dealers risk piling up
Article Text:
Traders and analysts have said that the slowdown in investment demand can be seen across silver exchange-traded funds (ETFs), bars and coins.

Silver Demand Weakens

Massive stockpiling of silver

Silver’s Spectacular Fall

(Disclaimer: Recommendations and views on the stock market, or any other asset classes or personal finance management tips given by experts and analysts are their own. These opinions do not represent the views of The Times of India.)

A huge crash in silver prices should have led to a revival in demand, but investors seem to be staying away. And this has raised a fresh worry ahead of the festive season.Silver refiners and bullion dealers are seeing their inventories build up as new investment demand for the metal weakens. The situation comes even as silver prices have dropped by more than 40% from their January peak of over Rs 4 lakh per kg. Uncertainty over a possible breakthrough in the US-Iran war and concerns about subdued industrial demand have added to the pressure.In Mumbai’s spot market, silver was trading at Rs 2.35 lakh per kg earlier this week.Traders and analysts have said that the slowdown in investment demand can be seen across silver exchange-traded funds (ETFs), bars and coins. Investors who bought the metal when prices were significantly higher are now sitting on substantial losses, making them hesitant to make fresh purchases despite the steep correction in prices!Also Read | A couple sold gold for Rs 20 lakh to buy a home, another family got Rs 80 lakh for a US degree and business: How Indians are unlocking value of idle gold sitting in their lockers "Investment demand for silver ETFs, bars and coins has come down. Internationally, prices are unlikely to cross $100 per troy ounce immediately unless the US-Iran war comes to an end. Silver prices are undervalued," Chirag Sheth, global business head, Public Gold Bullion (SG) Pte told ET. "The continuous war between US and Iran has impacted the solar industry, semiconductor industry and EV industry where silver is used. "The weak demand is also creating an inventory problem for domestic players.Indian bullion dealers and refiners have reportedly placed orders for around 2,000 tonnes of silver, which is currently in transit. The additional supplies have raised concerns over a further build-up in stocks. India imports around 7,000 tonnes of silver every year."With no new investors coming in and no immediate signs of prices going up, refiners and bullion dealers are facing a problem internationally as well as in domestic markets," said James Jose, president, Precious Metals Refiners Forum.Silver prices have fallen steadily over the past seven months, following an extraordinary rally that pushed the metal more than 300% higher year-on-year. In January, silver crossed Rs 4 lakh per kg on the Multi Commodity Exchange for the first time."The market is still digesting the aftermath of the speculation-driven frenzy, and this may be prompting investors to stay away after many of them incurred significant losses," said Carsten Menke, head, Next Generation Research, Julius Baer told ET.The outlook for industrial demand is adding to the pressure, with consumption expected to weaken. "A shift to cheaper alternatives, such as aluminium and copper, has started, and the growth outlook for Chinese solar module makers, which are the biggest industrial users of silver, is not as strong anymore," Menke said.The ongoing US-Iran war has added to the negative sentiment surrounding silver. If the conflict continues for an extended period, investors may remain cautious. At the same time, expectations of weaker industrial consumption could make a rapid rebound in silver prices difficult.Despite the sharp fall, some long-term investors are once again looking at silver as a way to diversify their portfolios."The market has taken full cognisance of the marked decline in silver prices in recent days. Some investors have shaved off their allocation, while others have prepared for fresh acquisition depending on their views and goals," said Nilanjan Dey, partner, Wishlist Capital.Dey said investors who have a time horizon of five years or longer may look at buying silver ETFs in a staggered manner instead of putting in a large amount at one go. Monthly or fortnightly investments could help spread out the purchase price and reduce the impact of short-term price movements.For first-time investors looking to add precious metals to their portfolios as a diversification from equities, ETFs can provide exposure without the need to hold or manage physical silver. However, Dey warned that investors with a shorter investment horizon should not assume that the recent decline automatically makes silver an attractive buying opportunity.
Article Summary: Silver refiners and bullion dealers are seeing their inventories build up as new investment demand for the metal weakens. Silver prices have dropped by more than 40% from their January peak of over Rs 4 lakh per kg. Uncertainty over a possible breakthrough in the US-Iran war and concerns about subdued industrial demand have added to the pressure.

Article Title: Travis Kelce’s $1.5 million nonprofit faces scrutiny after records show $469,000 spent on management and $446,000 on charity
Article Text:

Earlier this year, Travis Kelce ’s reputation for giving back was facing a setback after an investigation into the NFL players’ charitable foundations raised questions about how some donated money was spent. Kelce’s Eighty-Seven and Running Foundation raised more than $1.5 million between 2021 and 2024, yet its reported charity spending was notably lower than that of several other NFL-linked organizations.In January, 2026, according to federal tax records examined by The Arizona Republic, Eighty-Seven and Running reported about $1.5 million in revenue during the three-year period and roughly $1.1 million in expenses. About $446,000 was listed under charitable spending, while $469,000 was reported as management costs.That works out to about 41 cents of every dollar spent going toward charity based on the filings. Charity Navigator generally views nonprofits spending at least 70 cents of each dollar on programs as efficient, while CharityWatch uses 75 cents as a benchmark for high efficiency.The figures have drawn attention partly because of the foundation's ties to A&A Management Group.The company was co-founded by Travis Kelce’s longtime business managers, Aaron and André Eanes. Aaron Eanes also serves as the nonprofit’s executive director.Laurie Styron, executive director of CharityWatch, raised concerns about the structure after reviewing the records.“It appears to function more as an extension of the management company versus as an independent public charity,” said Laurie Styron, the executive director of CharityWatch, an independent charity watchdog group that reviewed the nonprofit’s tax filings for The Arizona Republic.“That’s not how charities work. It’s wrong.”..Travis Kelce’s team disputes the picture presented by the filings. Aaron Eanes said the reported figures did not properly classify some operational expenses tied to charitable work.“Operational costs for charitable efforts were “mistakenly reported under management rather than allocated adequately to program services,” Eanes told The Republic, so the public records do not provide an accurate “indication of where the resources were truly directed.”.Eanes said the foundation has since changed its approach, adding that management fees fell sharply in 2024 and reached zero in 2025. He also said the organization plans to expand its board, bring in nonprofit advisers and improve its reporting practices.“Looking ahead, we are expanding our board of directors, bringing on advisers with nonprofit expertise, and restructuring our reporting processes to better reflect our actual program work. We are dedicated to ensuring this foundation operates at the highest standards.”The scrutiny comes as the NFL continues to highlight charitable work through the Walter Payton NFL Man of the Year program. Kelce has been nominated three times and has supported causes in both Kansas City and his hometown of Cleveland.Kelce's foundation’s reported numbers do not erase that community work, but they do highlight why financial transparency matters. For celebrity-led nonprofits, public trust depends not only on how much money is raised, but also on how clearly and responsibly that money reaches the people it is meant to help.The foundation has since said it took steps to address the accounting and governance concerns, including changing how expenses were reported and eliminating management fees in 2025. However, there has been no public indication that the concerns raised by CharityWatch and The Arizona Republic have been formally cleared or independently resolved
Article Summary: Travis Kelce’s Eighty-Seven and Running Foundation raised more than $1.5 million between 2021 and 2024, yet its reported charity spending was notably lower than that of several other NFL-linked organizations. The figures have drawn attention partly because of the foundation's ties to A&A Management Group. The foundation has since said it took steps to address the accounting and governance concerns.

Article Title: RAKSHA Document : India unveils 10-year ‘RAKSHA’ roadmap to expand global defence & security ties
Article Text:
India looks to expand strategic defence ties under new ‘RAKSHA’ framework

Four key pillars of India's defence diplomacy roadmap

Strategic partnerships: Deepening bilateral and multilateral security cooperation.

Capacity building: Expanding joint military exercises, training programmes and the sharing of best practices with friendly nations.

Indigenous exports: Promoting Make-in-India defence platforms to position India as a reliable global defence manufacturing hub .

Senior officials attend release event

Rajnath Singh calls for stronger India-Belgium cooperation

Defence minister Rajnath Singh on Thursday released the ‘RAKSHA’ document on defence diplomacy, outlining India's strategic roadmap and vision for expanding global defence partnerships over the next 10 years.The document, unveiled at a special event in New Delhi, lays out a framework aimed at aligning India's national security objectives with proactive international cooperation, according to the ministry of defence.The strategic blueprint focuses on deepening bilateral and multilateral security ties, building capacity with friendly countries, promoting indigenous defence exports and strengthening maritime security.The ‘RAKSHA’ framework is built around four key pillars:The ministry of defence said the document provides a “clear, actionable vision” for the next decade as defence diplomacy remains a core pillar of India's foreign policy.The framework is aimed at ensuring India remains an anchor of peace, stability and a rules-based order in an evolving global landscape.Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth, defence secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh and secretary (defence production) Sanjeev Kumar were among the senior officials present at the event.Secretary (east) in the ministry of external affairs Rudrendra Tandon, Vice Chief of the Air Staff Air Marshal Ashutosh Dixit and Vice Chief of the Naval Staff Vice Admiral Ajay Kochhar also attended.The document was officially released during an event at Kartavya Bhawan.The directorate of public relations, ministry of defence, said in a post on X that the framework sets a 10-year roadmap to strengthen global security partnerships.“Aligning national security with proactive international cooperation, this comprehensive framework aims to position India as a key defence manufacturing hub and an anchor of regional stability,” it added.The document also seeks to strengthen India's role as a Net Security Provider and First Responder in the Indian Ocean Region, with defence diplomacy described as a core pillar of the country's foreign policy.The release came a day after India and Belgium held extensive discussions aimed at expanding bilateral defence and industrial cooperation.Singh hosted Belgian defence and trade minister Theo Francken in New Delhi on Wednesday, with multiple memorandums of understanding and contracts signed under defence industrial cooperation.“Had a very productive meeting with the Defence and Trade Minister of Belgium, Mr @FranckenTheo, in New Delhi today. We reviewed the entire spectrum of Defence relations and Defence Industrial Cooperation between India and Belgium. Multiple MoUs and contracts under the Defence Industrial Cooperation were also signed, towards leveraging Belgian technology together with Indian skill and scale,” Singh said.On Thursday, Singh called for greater cooperation between the two countries during the India-Belgium Ministers' Meeting in the national capital.“The world is witnessing a time of great geopolitical and economic turmoil. Most of it is not our doing, but we have to handle the challenges. In such situations, meeting a friend and partner like you provides a useful opportunity to exchange views and perspectives,” he said.Singh said the recently held India-Belgium Strategic Dialogue had provided a framework for taking the bilateral partnership forward, including in defence and security.
Article Summary: The document lays out a framework aimed at aligning India's national security objectives with proactive international cooperation. It focuses on deepening bilateral and multilateral security ties, building capacity with friendly countries, promoting indigenous defence exports and strengthening maritime security. The document was officially released during an event at Kartavya Bhawan.

Article Title: Can CP walk the talk on vehicle-free Inner Circle? NDMC chief seeks feedback
Article Text:
In photo: Inner Circle of Connaught Place





NEW DELHI: A fresh debate on the pedestrianisation of Connaught Place’s Inner Circle has begun after recently-appointed NDMC chairperson Manoj Kumar Dwivedi Thursday took to social media to invite suggestions on restricting vehicular movement in the area and making it more pedestrian-friendly.Dwivedi said every person in NCR would have visited CP at least once, and asked if a move like this should be implemented throughout the day or during specific hours.“Can we make the Inner Circle of CP vehicle-free so that people can walk around freely like on some mall roads or central areas in foreign cities? 2. Should we do it for a full day or do it from 6pm to midnight in summers and 11am to 4pm in winters? 3. Some different timing for weekends? 4. What kind of activities would you prefer in Central Park and Inner Circle during no vehicle slots? Positive suggestions would be appreciated,” he posted on X.While some welcomed the idea, others suggested that reforms should be carried out first. “Time slots are an excellent approach for the preliminary stage. Only suggestion is that the time slot for vehicle entry ban should not be during peak hours (for example 8-11am and 5-8pm), otherwise traffic snarls will stretch even further,” stated one user on ‘X’.Traders in CP opposed the proposal, saying it would impact revenue and worsen congestion. New Delhi Traders Association (NDTA) said restricting vehicle access directly in front of showrooms would hurt sales and diminish the accessibility of shops, restaurants and services.“Past trials resulted in sharp drops in footfall and chaotic parking conditions for genuine shoppers, especially children, women, senior citizens and the physically challenged. Also, closing Inner Circle will divert massive vehicular volumes onto Outer Circle and feeder roads, severely aggravating existing bottlenecks rather than eliminating congestion,” said NDTA president Atul Bhargava.Traders said NDTA should be consulted for any proposed changes in Connaught Place.“CP is already designed with 15 feet of covered corridors and 20 feet of walking space, making it inherently pedestrian-friendly without needing a vehicular restriction. Clearing the pedestrian corridors by removing hundreds of illegal hawkers and lifting wrongly parked buses, cabs and autos from roadsides will create enough space for pedestrians,” said Amit Gupta, member, NDTA.Traders also questioned whether there was enough parking space in CP to accommodate the large number of vehicles if entry to Inner Circle was restricted. Some also pointed out that the weather and pollution-free environment in other countries were different from Delhi, where walking on streets is often not feasible.This is not the first time that an attempt has been made or an idea floated to pedestrianise the area. In Jan 2017, former Union minister Venkaiah Naidu shared a plan to ‘pedestrianise’ CP on a pilot basis for three months, starting Feb.In 2019, former NDMC chairperson Naresh Kumar tried implementing a pilot project but faced resistance from traders, who later agreed to a two-day trial run. However, two days before the planned exercise, traders accused the agency of tweaking the plan and withdrew support.In April this year, LG TS Sandhu sought an action plan for pedestrianisation projects in high-footfall areas of CP and Khan Market to ensure essential civic services were provided.
Article Summary: NDMC chairperson Manoj Kumar Dwivedi invites suggestions on restricting vehicular movement in Connaught Place's Inner Circle. He asks if a move like this should be implemented throughout the day or during specific hours. New Delhi Traders Association (NDTA) says restricting vehicle access directly in front of showrooms would hurt sales.
